answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
Benefits:
- Rewards companies that go the extra mile. Consequential accounting makes visible the difference between actions that merely shift accounting results and those that genuinely decarbonise the grid. In an increasingly anti-ESG geopolitical context, this method allows companies to demonstrate measurable, real-world climate benefits instead of symbolic or compliance-only actions. It rewards proactive firms willing to take harder, higher-impact steps, providing stronger legitimacy and resilience against ESG backlash.

- Reduces greenwashing and over-crediting. It avoids misleading “paper” reductions, often due to EF changes, by ensuring that reported results reflect true avoided emissions. This strengthens the credibility of corporate climate claims and builds trust with regulators, investors, and the public.

- Enhances transparency, policy alignment, and long-term systems thinking
Consequential accounting can align corporate actions with national decarbonisation pathways and energy transition models, ensuring consistency between private and public efforts. By considering how projects affect the future grid – such as influencing fossil retirements, curtailment, or firm capacity needs – it promotes a long-term, system-oriented view of decarbonisation rather than a narrow, short-term accounting perspective.

- Improves capital efficiency and innovation. By linking emissions outcomes to time and location, companies can compare interventions by cost per tonne of CO2 avoided and focus investment on technologies such as storage, demand flexibility, or 24/7 clean energy that deliver higher system value. For example, it supports battery storage in regions with already high volumes of solar (such as California, Spain, or Chile), where shifting surplus midday solar into evening peaks directly reduces gas or coal use.

Challenges:
- Baselines and reporting complexity. Annual reporting of consequential reductions relies on annually updated marginal emission rates, as grid conditions and models evolve. This is methodologically sound but adds data and modelling burden, and can create volatility in reported impacts from year to year.

- Method standardisation, data, and governance. Different model types, temporal resolution, treatment of curtailment, and emission-factor vintages can lead to materially different results for similar projects, so minimum methodological requirements, transparent assumptions, open datasets where possible, and clear rules on version control and restatements are essential for comparability and assurance.

- System boundaries and leakage. Consequential estimates are highly sensitive to how system boundaries are drawn, including interconnection flows, cycling and start-up/shut-down of thermal units, and capacity or retirement dynamics; if these are not handled consistently, analyses may overstate net system reductions by focusing on local displacement rather than overall system behaviour.

- Attribution and double counting. As utilities, corporate buyers, aggregators, DR providers, and storage owners all participate in the same underlying system changes, robust attribution rules are needed so that only one set of actors claims each avoided MWh or tonne of CO2, based on contractual rights, metered performance, or clear dispatch and ownership principles.

- Cost and expertise requirements. High-quality consequential analysis is data- and expertise-intensive, which raises costs for users, especially outside well-modelled markets, and requires clear guidance on when simplified approaches are acceptable versus when full modelling is expected.

Unintended consequences:
- There is a reputational risk if vendor methods or grid models are revised and previously reported consequential impacts need to be restated, potentially undermining trust in corporate climate claims.

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text: Yes. The Scope 2 TWG formula is structurally appropriate because it follows the same core logic as the Guidelines (electricity volume × marginal emission rate summed over time) in a simplified, hourly form suitable for annual ex post reporting. It clearly quantifies only primary grid effects, which is acceptable as long as the standard explicitly states this boundary and explains how any optional secondary-effect analysis would sit alongside this core equation.

answers.label: Secondary effects to consider, and how
answers.text: Secondary effects should be treated in line with the existing Guidelines

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text:
Reporting each year is the most practical approach for broad uptake because it aligns with how companies already manage governance, assurance, and disclosure cycles, and it scales across portfolios of actions rather than creating a one-off modelling exercise for each project. It also avoids locking in a lifetime impact number that depends on long-range assumptions about grid evolution and counterfactuals, which can become outdated quickly and be hard to assure consistently across reporters.

Annual reporting also supports continuous improvement as marginal emission rate datasets and methodologies mature. It allows organisations to automate recurring calculations once the data pipeline is established, and to reflect changes in project operation and system conditions over time, rather than having to defend a single estimate made at project outset. If useful for decision-making, a one-time lifetime estimate can still be used internally as a supplementary planning metric, but the standard reporting approach should be annual.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
Regulatory test - Optional
Do not make this a required test. In environments like the US, where climate and ESG policy can swing with administrations, using “not legally required” as a mandatory gate risks rewarding low-ambition or actively regressive policy. The regulatory test is still useful as a negative screen (to exclude capacity that is directly mandated), but it should not be the main proof of additionality and should stay optional, combined with other tests.

Timing test - Required
Simple, objective, and politically neutral. Ensures very old or fully pre-financed projects are not counted as newly additional.

Contractual / tenor test - Required
Also politically neutral. A minimum level of contractual commitment (tenor, volume, or revenue support) is a strong, observable signal that the buyer’s action is plausibly influencing investment.

Positive list – Optional, but highly feasible.
Positive lists are already used in schemes like RE100, so for many buyers it is straightforward to show that a project falls into an approved category. However, because not all regions or actors are covered by existing lists, and lists can become outdated as markets evolve, it is better to treat them as an easy optional route to demonstrate additionality rather than a universal requirement.

Financial, barrier, common practice, and performance standards can help show additionality in some cases, but they are often data heavy, subjective, or hard to apply everywhere. “First-of-its-kind” doesn’t add much beyond the others and is not needed to show a project is additional.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text:
Common practice, performance standard, both require market data and careful boundary setting but are widely used in carbon standards and can be implemented where robust statistics exist but not in all markets.

Financial and barrier tests demand granular project data, developer cooperation, and expert judgement, which can be costly and inconsistent across regions. First-of-its-kind adds little beyond these and can be hard to define objectively, so should not be central to the framework.

answers.label: Regions warranting different tests, with examples
answers.text: In mature, policy-driven markets with high renewable penetration (for example parts of Western Europe or some US ISOs), stricter tests such as timing, common practice or performance benchmarks, and contractual tests are needed to distinguish truly additional projects from business-as-usual build. In emerging or weaker-policy markets (for example some African or South Asian grids), simpler regulatory tests combined with positive lists and basic timing tests may be more appropriate, to avoid excluding projects that are clearly additional but lack detailed data.

answers.label: Claims possible under different test approaches
answers.text:
For association-type claims (for example “our procurement supports renewables in region X”), a lighter set of tests could be sufficient - for instance regulatory and timing tests plus a basic contractual screen.

For strong causal claims (for example “our contract enabled this project” or quantified avoided emissions claims), a higher bar should apply, combining regulatory, timing, contractual/tenor, and at least one of financial, performance, or common practice tests. This tiered approach aligns the cost and complexity of additionality assessment with the strength of the claim being made.
